item.title: QE ArXiv Watch: Week of November 16 - November 23, 2026
item.description:
# QE ArXiv Watch Weekly Week ending November 23, 2026

The clever move this week: measure what ordinary designs miss

A control chart can miss a process change even when every sensor still looks normal on its own. Nascimento and colleagues’ C_n-chart looks instead at the joint density of the sensor readings—so an unusual relationship between otherwise familiar measurements can trigger an alarm. That’s a useful reminder running through this week’s papers: better decisions often come not from collecting more data, but from choosing observations that reveal the structure we care about.

The chart fits distributions to individual sensor measurements, joins them with a copula, then flags observations whose estimated joint density is unusually low. In a simulated dependence reversal, it detected the change in an average of 8.1 observations, versus 48 for a calibrated Hotelling T^2 chart and 227 for separate marginal charts. The theoretical in-control average run length is exactly 1/α when the baseline parameters are known and observations are independent. In practice, Phase I estimation matters: with a target run length of 200, some reported simulations fell short, especially with only 100 baseline observations. Still, the computation looks promising for sensor applications: fitting at 20 variables took under a minute in the reported tests, and scoring 10,000 new observations took at most 0.23 seconds.

Designing experiments around the information you need

Three of the DOE papers tackle a familiar engineering problem from different angles: how to get more useful information from a limited experimental budget.

For online A/B testing, Gupta et al. optimize action-level sampling probabilities alongside a reward-prediction control variate. In simulations, their design reached the mean squared error of a balanced test using just 39–51% of its traffic, and delivered 1.5–2.1 times the power at 10,000 interactions. That’s especially relevant when tests are costly or traffic is scarce. The results are simulation-based, though; teams will want to validate the reward model and design on their own historical data before trusting the savings.

For computer experiments, Pronzato et al. focus on average distance from a random point in the domain to its nearest design point—a different goal from simply avoiding close pairs or covering the worst gap. Their high-dimensional designs use carefully selected hypercube vertices, with fractional-factorial subsets and greedy selection helping build strong intermediate designs. The practical wrinkle: good coverage of the full space can trade off against good low-dimensional projections. If downstream analysis depends on particular factors or slices, inspect those projections rather than relying on a single space-filling score.

Network experiments have their own version of the coverage problem. Liu et al.’s FANCI sequentially chooses network-and-treatment combinations to learn how outcomes vary with neighborhood exposure. In simulations, after seven experiments it substantially outperformed random selection and a maximum-model-change benchmark at recovering overall and spillover effects. Their online-game study also found exposure-dependent effects that a model ignoring interference could not represent. For quality engineers working with connected systems—plants, suppliers, or users—this is a reminder that one unit’s treatment can change another’s outcome.

Finally, Shamekh et al. ask which time-series observations make dynamical-model parameters identifiable. In Lorenz-96, adding measurements of the fast field to a short record of slow variables sharply improved recovery of fast-process parameters. The broader lesson travels well: before extending a measurement campaign, ask whether you’re observing the variables and time scales that distinguish the competing explanations.

This week’s common thread is thoughtful allocation: of sensor attention, test traffic, design points, networks, and measurement time. Where in your process are we collecting plenty of data—but not the data that can tell us what changed?

Featured Papers This Week

  • Nascimento et al.: Sensor Monitoring Towards Industry 4.0: Bridging Concepts on the $C_n$ Multivariate Control Chart (SPM)
  • Gupta et al.: Variance-Optimal Counterfactual Policy Design for Sample-Efficient Online A/B Testing (DOE)
  • Pronzato et al.: Sparse designs via quantization of the uniform measure on high-dimensional hypercubes (DOE)
  • Liu et al.: Fill-Distance-Guided Active Learning for Causal Function Recovery under Network Interference (DOE)

item.title: QE ArXiv Watch: Week of November 09 - November 16, 2026
item.description:
# QE ArXiv Watch Weekly Week ending November 16, 2026 · 5 papers

What if we could get a useful materials-strength model with a third fewer tests? That’s the enticing result from this week’s standout: a sequential design method for high-entropy alloys that chooses experiments based on how much they could improve predictions—not just where the model is most uncertain.

Raihan et al.’s ROSE-HEA was tested retrospectively on 501 alloy records. Starting with 25 observations and adding 100 strategically selected ones, it achieved a mean RMSE of 152.84 MPa across 30 runs. More striking for a lab watching its test budget: with 125 observations, it beat the strongest conventional regressor in the comparison trained on 185. That’s a promising signal for expensive experimental programs, though retrospective results are not the same as a prospective lab trial. The useful idea is broader: choose the next test for its impact on predictions across the region you care about, rather than chasing uncertainty in isolation.

There’s a nice companion question in the paper by Idais et al.: when do we need to redesign the experiment because our model parameters are uncertain? For single-factor Poisson, gamma, and logistic models, the answer depends on the model and how diffuse the prior uncertainty is. The gamma endpoint design stayed optimal across all priors they considered. For Poisson and logistic models, local designs held up under concentrated priors, but diffuse priors favored designs with three support points; the original designs then lost some efficiency. In practice, “use the textbook optimal design” may be fine when your prior knowledge is tight—but uncertainty in the model parameters can change where you should sample.

Two other DOE papers widen the lens from where to measure to what an experiment should include. Lacasa et al. offer a Bayesian way to detect spatial structure that the planned blocks in an agricultural field may have missed. In simulations, their treatment-effect intervals had close-to-nominal 95% coverage, and their wheat and corn examples revealed additional spatial patterns. That’s a useful reminder: a carefully randomized design can still sit on top of an imperfect map of field variability.

Meanwhile, MineralExp puts LLM agents to a practical test: can they plan geochemical experiments for mineral exploration? The agents generally found many of the experiments called for, but often proposed too many. One setup reached 86% recall while precision was about 32%—in other words, it caught most of the target but generated a lot of extra work. More tokens didn’t reliably mean better plans, either. For engineers considering AI-assisted planning, the benchmark makes a valuable distinction between “suggests something relevant” and “produces a focused, usable plan.”

The reliability paper moves from designing experiments to understanding system behavior. Torrado et al. derive a decomposition showing how dependence changes k-out-of-n reliability relative to an independent-components benchmark. Their illustration shows that higher-order dependence can matter even when pairwise dependence is held fixed. The reported structural weights are not measured reliability changes; they tell us how strongly the system architecture and threshold can amplify a specified dependence contribution.

Across the week, a common thread is that good decisions depend on more than a single uncertainty score or model assumption. Whether we’re choosing the next alloy test, accounting for field patterns, or assessing component dependence, the structure of the problem matters. Where in your own process might a “small” modeling assumption be steering a costly decision?

Featured Papers This Week

  • Raihan et al.: Sample-efficient prediction of high-entropy alloy strength through outcome-aware robust sequential learning (DOE)
  • Wang et al.: MineralExp: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Experimental Design in Real-World Mineral Exploration (DOE)
  • Torrado et al.: Quantifying Dependence Effects on $k$-out-of-$n$ Reliability Relative to the Independent Benchmark (Reliability)
  • Lacasa et al.: A Bayesian approach for checking and estimating block designs in agricultural experiments (DOE)

item.title: QE ArXiv Watch: Week of November 02 - November 09, 2026
item.description:
# QE ArXiv Watch Weekly Week ending November 09, 2026

The most striking result this week is a reminder that nuisance parameters can change more than the fine print: they can change how much data you need. In software reliability, allowing an unknown trend in detection effort shifts the failure count needed to detect population depletion from roughly N^{2/3} to N^{4/5}. If your test plan assumes the trend away, you may think you have evidence of finite-population effects long before you really do.

Designs you can build—and designs you can adapt

For order-of-addition experiments, Georgiou et al. give a satisfying exact result: start with an orthogonal array, add one order, and the enlarged design is determinant-optimal among designs of that run size. For foldover designs, the corresponding optimal augmentation is a reversal pair. This is stronger than a good heuristic: the comparison allows replication and replacing original runs. It gives practitioners a principled way to add a small number of runs when a study grows, rather than rebuilding from scratch. One useful caveat: deleting a reversal pair need not produce a determinant-optimal smaller design, even when it meets a discrepancy bound.

Kerrigan et al.’s open-source TESTBED tackles a different design challenge: comparing Bayesian experimental-design strategies across problems. Its modular setup lets you mix models, objectives, and optimization methods, including sequential designs. The benchmark’s practical lesson is that no strategy wins everywhere—and implementation details matter. On one location-finding task, giving an adaptive policy explicit time information made a large difference. That’s a good nudge to scrutinize what information your policy receives, not just which algorithm you choose.

Two papers help connect these applied methods to broader ideas. Tarek et al. show how familiar criteria—D-, T-, A-, C-, and E-optimality—can be read through divergences and distances between prior and posterior beliefs. It’s a theoretical bridge, not a new performance benchmark, but it clarifies what different criteria are “trying” to optimize. Obando et al. put expected information gain to work in single-pixel imaging: an RL policy learns adaptive illumination patterns, recovering the optimal bisection strategy in a small, noiseless one-active-pixel setting. Promising as a proof of concept; not yet evidence for general images or hardware.

Reliability: use what you have, but model what you don’t

Chaudhuri et al. review multifidelity tools for rare-event and tail-risk estimation. The idea is familiar from production modeling: use cheaper, imperfect simulations to guide or correct expensive ones. Control variates, importance sampling, and active learning each exploit that relationship differently. The review reports no new benchmark, so treat “orders of magnitude” cost reductions as motivation, not a guarantee for your system. The payoff depends on whether low-fidelity models are informative about the risk quantity you care about.

For reliability data scattered across sources, Ortiz et al. combine failure-rate distributions under a constant-rate assumption. Their simulations suggest moment matching works well when sources are homogeneous; minimizing KL divergence is a better choice when heterogeneity is present or uncertain. That’s a practical distinction when aggregating sparse equipment records—but the real-data application doesn’t establish predictive accuracy.

Together, this week’s papers keep returning to a useful question: before we optimize a design or pool more data, what assumptions—and nuisance structure—are quietly setting the limits of what we can learn?

  • Georgiou et al.: Exact optimality of augmented order-of-addition designs (DOE)

item.title: QE ArXiv Watch: Week of October 26 - November 02, 2026
item.description:
# QE ArXiv Watch Weekly Week ending November 02, 2026

The best design isn’t always the one that covers the space most evenly. This week’s papers keep asking a more practical question: what uncertainty are we trying to reduce, and what assumptions are we willing to trust? That’s a useful shift for anyone designing experiments where runs are costly, measurements are clustered, or the system keeps changing under our feet.

The most immediately portable idea comes from Karl et al.’s sphericity filter for nondeterministic experiments. It starts with a familiar goal—choose a space-filling design—but also protects precision for effects we think may matter. Across their examples, that small change often bought better prediction precision at modest geometric cost. In a constrained lipid-nanoparticle study, efficiency improved 27.5% over a geometry-focused comparator, with a 2.3% increase in median geometric cost. The catch is important: the filter needs a working model to say which effects to protect. In the same study, a raw coefficient-based filter actually reduced efficiency. So this is a promising way to refine a candidate design, not a license to treat the model as unquestionable.

Cao et al. offer a quieter but equally practical reminder from oat trials: plants from the same plot are not independent experimental units. Their Bayesian ordinal model accounts for ordered growth stages and plot-level clustering, then compares models by holding out whole plots. Leaving out the plot effect substantially hurt prediction and made some contrast intervals look narrower than they should. By contrast, adding a spatial field provided little detectable benefit on these layouts. For quality engineers, the lesson travels well: model the randomization and sampling structure first; add spatial complexity when the data can support it.

Zanotta et al.’s FIDE takes design selection into less familiar territory: measurements of evolving population laws, where aggregate observations can’t identify the full state. FIDE first enforces a scientific-risk allowance, then prefers designs that require a smaller correction to a frozen reference dynamics. That preference improved held-out action measures in several simulations, including a 32-dimensional example. But it is explicitly reference-dependent: when the baseline was misspecified, its downstream advantage could reverse. Think of it as a way to choose among designs given a trusted reference, not as protection against a bad one.

And then there’s Moradi et al., who put experimental design on one athlete’s training schedule. EPICOACH proposes feasible workouts that balance learning about the rider with improving performance, while recording predictions before the rides—an appealing discipline for any adaptive system. The results are a good reality check: heart-rate forecasts improved over several baselines, but segment-time forecasts did not, and early climb forecasts missed the athlete’s improvement. Safety checks also vetoed the top-ranked overload plan in both live cycles. That’s not a failure of the idea; it’s a reminder that a clever experiment planner still needs a model that can keep up with a changing process.

Across the week, the common thread is design for the decision you actually care about—and make your assumptions visible. Which assumption in your own experiment would you most want to stress-test before trusting the design?

  • Moradi et al.: The Athlete as a Scientist of One: Agentic Bayesian Experimental Design for Individualized Physiology from Consumer Wearables (DOE)

item.title: QE ArXiv Watch: Week of October 19 - October 26, 2026
item.description:
# QE ArXiv Watch Weekly Week ending October 26, 2026

This week’s useful reminder: getting to an answer sooner is only a win if we know what risk we’re taking to get there. Two papers tackle that trade-off in online experiments from different angles—and a reliability study shows why a “best” maintenance age can be much less certain than its cost estimate suggests.

Faster A/B tests, with the guardrails made explicit. Perini et al. build group sequential designs that can stop an experiment early while retaining the platform’s fixed-horizon terminal decision rule. Their predictive-probability stopping policy cut expected duration by 41.7% in simulation; online experiments showed a 43.1% runtime reduction and an estimated 76% increase in testing capacity. The practical appeal is clear: less waiting without quietly loosening error-rate or power targets. But the policy’s boundaries and horizon are chosen by simulation, so teams should validate them against their own traffic patterns and outcome correlations.

Lu et al. address a different trap: repeatedly checking a clustered experiment’s quantile results. Their CAQ method provides sequential confidence sequences for quantile effects when users contribute multiple correlated events. In simulations, cumulative miscoverage stayed around 3%, while “peek at a fixed-horizon test” and “ignore clustering” baselines failed badly. CAQ’s validity is asymptotic, not an exact finite-sample guarantee; still, it’s a promising option when tail behavior matters and experiments are monitored continuously.

Maintenance decisions need risk ranges, not just a point estimate. Wu et al. model changing inter-failure times with a geometric process and quantify uncertainty in both reliability and replacement age. In an aircraft example with just 27 intervals, two strategies at cycle 9 had cost rates of 12.705 and 13.767—but reliabilities of 0.912 and 0.670. That’s a striking reminder that modest expected-cost differences can conceal substantial risk differences. Their generalized confidence intervals had better coverage than bootstrap and Bayesian intervals in several small-sample simulations. For practitioners, the message is to show decision-makers the reliability consequences of a replacement policy, not only its average cost.

A useful counterpoint to this week’s enthusiasm for adaptive methods comes from Nyaupane et al., who audit learned experimental-design controllers. In one simulated voltage-clamp task, policies presented as learned feedback controllers always chose the same protocol; masking the observed current changed nothing. In a task where the best next pulse truly depended on the first observation, they did adapt—and matched a Bayesian reference. Clever algorithms can use feedback, but we should test whether the feedback actually changes decisions and improves outcomes.

The remaining papers focus on getting the design right for messy experiments. Zhang et al. show how rerandomization and Lasso adjustment can sharpen network-effect estimates, while accounting for auxiliary variables that themselves depend on assignment. Singh et al. tackle therapist capacity, availability, and turnover: flexible allocation can substantially reduce the number of batches needed, though no strategy dominates across settings. And Kaji et al. offer a two-stage design for multi-arm trials with noncompliance, identifying a targeted local effect under specific assumptions about treatment choice and receipt.

Across the week, the common thread is operational realism: clustering, interference, scarce staff, noncompliance, changing failure rates. The question for us is not simply whether a method is adaptive or efficient. It’s whether its assumptions match the system we’re trying to improve.

Featured Papers This Week

  • Lu et al.: CAQ: Clustered Asymptotically Anytime-Valid Quantile Treatment Effects for Online Experiments (DOE)

item.title: QE ArXiv Watch: Week of October 12 - October 19, 2026
item.description:
# QE ArXiv Watch Weekly Week ending October 19, 2026

The experiment is only as good as the decision it feeds

Here’s a useful twist on experimental design: the best experiment may not be the one that teaches us the most. If a downstream decision rule can’t use the information well—or uses it in a way that conflicts with our goals—more data can actually make outcomes worse.

That’s the central idea in Iqbal et al.’s Designing Experiments for External Decision Makers. Their usage-aware designs account for the rule that will act on the results, whether it’s a familiar statistical test, a black box, or a cautious human decision-maker. In manufacturing inspection, the learned policy’s mean loss was 0.265, versus 0.414 for the best baseline. The practical prompt is simple: before optimizing what to measure, ask what someone will do with the measurement.

A related lesson comes from Rewarding Noise, which looks at the incentives embedded in A/B-test scoring rules. When teams are rewarded for raw estimates, lucky noise can look like product impact. In Amazon data, a shift to posterior-mean-based evaluation coincided with fewer tests, lower standard errors, and tests aimed at ideas with more variable impacts. Estimated testing value rose, but the scoring change also came with a change in launch criteria—so don’t credit the scoring rule alone.

Better experiments need better operations

In trials of therapist-delivered interventions, Singh et al. show why a tidy factorial design can be awkward in the real world: therapists have limited capacity, availability changes, and people leave. Flexible allocation strategies often needed far fewer batches than restrictive approaches, while randomizing therapists to patients helped avoid badly biased estimates of therapist variability. There’s no one-size-fits-all winner; the design has to match the staffing and timing constraints.

Kaji et al. tackle a different trial complication: people don’t always receive the treatment they’re assigned. Their proposed two-stage design uses participants’ stated favorite arm to help identify certain local treatment effects. It’s a clever theoretical route, but its assumptions about preferences and compliance matter, and the paper doesn’t yet test the design in a live experiment.

For practitioners building sequential experiments, Kriz et al. train a reasoning LLM to choose informative questions. In a Twenty Questions setting, expected-reward training improved both information gain and solve rate over the comparison training approach. More provocatively, Liu et al.’s causal-discovery benchmark finds that agents’ main failure is often not interpreting evidence—it’s choosing experiments that produce useful evidence. Capping the size of each data request prompted more controlled experiments and improved exact recovery. That’s a reminder for human teams, too: disciplined data collection can beat simply buying more observations.

One quieter result with practical value: Shan et al. establish when balanced six-factor experimental arrays exist. It’s a theoretical design-tool contribution, not a performance study, but it helps clarify when pairwise-balanced plans are feasible without extra runs.

Reliability: model what changes, not just what fails

For multivariate degradation, Niu et al. model both shared environmental damage and unit-to-unit differences. In a small epoxy-coating example, their age-based replacement policy cut the reported long-run cost rate by about 66% versus waiting for failure. Treat that application cautiously—just four specimens—but the modeling lesson is strong: shared degradation and heterogeneity can matter to maintenance timing.

Janetzky et al. address another real production headache: new configurations arrive, while old ones may return. A progressive neural network trained on Bosch manufacturing data reduced maintenance costs relative to fine-tuning and per-configuration models, while retaining information across configurations. That’s promising when retraining from all historical data isn’t practical.

Across this week’s papers, the common thread is a shift from “collect better data” to “design for the system that will use it.” Where in your own process are our experiments optimized for a statistic, rather than for the decision that statistic is supposed to support?

item.title: QE ArXiv Watch: Week of October 05 - October 12, 2026
item.description:
# QE ArXiv Watch Weekly Week ending October 12, 2026

What if your experiment could stop early, keep its error guarantees while you peek at the results, and still estimate effects precisely? One paper this week gets close—and it points to a broader theme across the batch: good design can do more than improve precision. It can make inference faster, more reliable, and easier to operationalize.

Yu et al. build a method for multifactor online experiments that combines treatment allocation, continuous monitoring, and estimation. Their block-orthogonal designs separate treatment information from nuisance block effects, while an anytime-valid e-value lets teams monitor evidence without invalidating their test by checking repeatedly. In simulations, the procedure stopped after an average of 1.4 batches, versus 7.7 for a safe-testing competitor, and had lower treatment-effect estimation error. In a 128-response prompt experiment, it stopped at batch four while the alternatives ran to the end. The practical draw is especially clear when experiments are expensive: orthogonal arrays can also cut a seven-factor design from 128 runs to 16 while preserving the design’s key properties. The reported type-I error was 5.8%, so—as always with a new procedure—teams should check how its guarantees and operating characteristics fit their own setting.

For causal experiments with complicated assignment schemes, Klosin et al. offer a refreshingly practical variance estimator. Their connected-components approach uses the pattern of which potential outcomes can’t be observed together to build an unbiased estimate of an upper bound on design-based variance. It reduces to familiar estimators under complete and cluster randomization, but can be much sharper in more tangled designs. In a school-network application, it gave the shortest standard error in seven of eight specifications; some competing calculations took hours, while theirs took under a second. If your treatment assignments are dependent—because of networks, geography, or other design constraints—this looks worth a closer read.

Two cautions from Zaidi et al. are useful for anyone running online tests on skewed outcomes. Blocking on a pre-experiment scale measure reduced variance in their simulations, with finer blocks producing larger gains. But handling the tails matters: within-block winsorization improved precision while maintaining coverage in a tail-effect scenario, whereas global winsorization and inverse-variance weighting produced badly calibrated results. The latter is a good reminder that a tiny standard error is no comfort if the analysis has quietly changed the estimand.

The remaining papers extend the design conversation in different directions. Yin et al. ask how far mobile sensors must move when the signal model changes. Their certification method can bound movement when the model perturbation is small and the placement objective has enough separation; the key message is that perturbation size alone won’t guarantee stability. Liu et al. show, theoretically, that LinUCB’s adaptive sampling can approach D-optimal designs in a small-gap regime—suggesting an algorithm built for regret reduction can also be information-efficient.

Across this week’s work, design is increasingly treated as part of inference, not just a setup step. The question for practitioners: where could a better allocation—or a better account of dependence—save more than just sample size?

Featured Papers This Week

  • Klosin et al.: Simple Standard Errors for Complicated (Quasi-)Experimental Designs (DOE)
  • Zaidi et al.: On the Benefit of Blocking for Online Experiments with Skewed Data (DOE)

item.title: QE ArXiv Watch: Week of September 28 - October 05, 2026
item.description:
The most quietly radical idea this week: stop pretending your estimator is smooth and your measurement plan is “information-matrix optimal.”

If you’re selecting sensors, test points, pixels, or inspections because downstream you’ll run Lasso / elastic net / TV denoising, then classical A- and D-optimality can be aiming at the wrong target. Marques et al. basically say: design for what you actually deploy, not for a Gaussian-linear fairy tale.

Designing measurements for nonsmooth reality (and doing it without pain)

Marques et al. tackle a practitioner-shaped problem: we want a small subset of measurements, but our inference pipeline is nonsmooth. In that world, “maximize det(Fisher info)” can be like optimizing a car for top speed when you’re actually driving in snow.

Their move is bilevel experimental design: the lower level solves the exact nonsmooth estimator you’ll use; the upper level chooses which measurements to buy by minimizing a validation-style prediction risk—without needing ground-truth signals. Sparsity comes from continuous acquisition weights in [0,1]^M plus a concave “price” penalty, and they trace the whole budget–performance frontier via a price homotopy (multiple usable designs per run, not one design per budget).

What’s nice for us: they avoid the usual “differentiate through an argmin that’s nonsmooth” trap with a value-function penalty and a single-loop proximal-gradient method, with an O(1/K) stationarity guarantee under reasonable conditions.

The results are the kind that matter when budgets are tight: in sparse regression with <40 sensors, median test NMSE drops ~40% versus D-/A-optimal; in Fashion-MNIST pixel selection with ≤32 pixels, they beat every baseline in every paired comparison—massively. At high budgets they converge toward “random is fine,” which is also useful guidance: don’t over-engineer when you’ve already bought plenty of signal.

Zero-label “design,” but for eliciting priors from an LLM

Teng et al. isn’t DOE in the traditional sense, but the vibe is familiar: choose a small set of queries to efficiently learn a response surface. MARS builds a tabular classifier with zero task labels by asking an LLM for feature-level log-odds at representative “anchor” values (quantiles/categories), then interpolating into per-feature response functions. After that, prediction is just an additive score—no test-time LLM calls.

If you’re doing quality triage with weak/no labels and you can articulate domain priors in language (“higher vibration RMS strongly increases failure odds after X”), MARS is an intriguing bridge. It’s also refreshingly cost-aware: reported API spend is ~10% of a heavier baseline, with modest gains from repeated elicitation (R=1→5).

Reliability: the claim is the product

Two reliability papers land the same punch from different angles: reliability isn’t a number, it’s a statement with assumptions.

Hardy et al. show why “just add more tasks” doesn’t necessarily fix agent benchmark noise. Using Generalizability Theory with Bayesian mixed models, they separate what you think you’re measuring (model quality) from what you’re often measuring (model+scaffold system quality). System ranking reliability is very high; underlying-model ranking reliability can be awful—and scaffold choice can reorder models. The practical takeaway for anyone running internal leaderboards: if your evaluation pipeline (prompting/tooling/scaffold) varies, you may be ranking your harness more than your model. Also: pooling diverse benchmarks can buy more reliability per dollar than deepening one benchmark.

Boland et al. make the analogous point for power-system adequacy: expected unserved energy (USE) misses tail risk when renewables correlate. They propose a modular “metric factory” (transform + time aggregation + risk functional) that produces interpretable standards like CVaR of USE, tail probability of max outage, outage duration distributions, etc. If you manage reliability risk, you want more than one lens—especially one that can see the tail.

Pan et al. zoom out and argue for an AI reliability engineering program built around a “reliability triangle”: failure definition, operational envelope, and evidence. The useful bit for QE folks is how classical tools map over: exposure-adjusted recurrent-event models (don’t rank by raw counts), overdispersion handling, accelerated/adversarial testing framed as reliability growth, and controls aligned to where failures live (component vs operational loop vs agentic conduct vs governance).

One question to sit with

Across sensors, benchmarks, grids, and agents, the trend is the same: optimize and report against the thing you actually claim—not the convenient proxy.

So: in your world, what’s the proxy you’ve been optimizing because it was easy to compute—and what would change if you optimized the deployed decision rule instead?

item.title: QE ArXiv Watch: Week of September 21 - September 28, 2026
item.description:
The most useful reminder from this week’s lone submission: when you’re chasing failure probabilities like 10⁻⁶, “just run more Monte Carlo” isn’t a plan — it’s a budget bonfire. Sharma et al. pull together 10–15 years of structural reliability work and, in the process, give us a very pragmatic map of which rare‑event tool to reach for depending on geometry, dimension, and whether time is part of the failure definition.

If you do reliability work in any domain (structures, aerospace, energy, complex mechanical systems), the storyline will feel familiar: we’re trying to estimate vanishingly small failure probabilities under messy nonlinear limit states, often with high-dimensional uncertainty. Practitioners care because these are exactly the regimes where qualification-by-testing breaks down and naive simulation becomes impossible. The review even puts a number on the pain: to estimate P_F ≈ 10^{-6} with ~10% relative error, crude Monte Carlo can push you toward ~10⁸ samples. That’s not “overnight on the cluster”; that’s “rethink the method.”

What’s nice is how the review organizes the ecosystem:

1) Fast approximations (FORM/SORM) still matter — but only when they’re honest. For time-invariant problems with relatively smooth limit states, FORM/SORM remain attractive as a first pass: cheap, interpretable, and often good enough for screening or sensitivity. But the review doesn’t oversell them: weird failure-domain geometry, multiple disjoint failure regions, or strong nonlinearity can make “a single most probable failure point” a brittle assumption.

2) Importance sampling is your scalpel — if you can aim it. The survey walks through adaptive IS, cross-entropy (CE) tuning, directional IS, and (for stochastic dynamics) Girsanov-based changes of measure. The subtext: IS works beautifully when you can learn a good proposal distribution, and it struggles when the failure set is multi-modal or hard to discover. If you’ve ever “improved” Monte Carlo only to discover you aimed at the wrong failure mode, you’ll feel seen.

3) Splitting / Subset Simulation is the workhorse for ugly rare events. Subset Simulation and cousins get highlighted as particularly practical when failure is rare and geometry is complicated. A detail worth stealing: the typical intermediate conditional probability choice p_0 ≈ 0.1–0.3 shows up again, with literature suggesting p_0 ≈ 0.2 is near-optimal for coefficient of variation. That’s the kind of rule-of-thumb engineers actually use.

4) ML surrogates are moving from “speed trick” to “search strategy.” Surrogate modeling + active learning is framed less as “replace physics with a black box” and more as “spend expensive evaluations only where they change the failure probability estimate.” There’s also a nod to generative models for load simulation — early days, but aligned with the trend we’re seeing: learning realistic extremes without handcrafting distributions.

One thread I’d love to see QE folks borrow more aggressively: embedding variance reduction into experimental qualification, not just computation. The review cites prior work estimating probabilities as low as ~5 × 10^{-5} with ~1750 controlled shake-table samples — basically, “design the experiment like an importance sampler.”

The question to sit with this week: In your reliability workflow, are we still treating rare-event estimation as a simulation problem, when it’s really a search-and-allocation problem? The methods that win aren’t just faster — they’re better at finding where failure actually lives.

item.title: QE ArXiv Watch: Week of September 14 - September 21, 2026
item.description:
QE ArXiv Watch Weekly — Week ending Sep 21, 2026 (4 papers)

If you’ve ever tried to “validate” a gen‑AI workflow with the same instincts you use for gage R&R or reliability growth, this week has a satisfying theme: stop treating evaluation as a leaderboard exercise and start treating it as an evidence-and-uncertainty problem. That shows up in enterprise LLM rollouts, medical forecasting, and rare-event probability estimation.

When “it looks good” isn’t decision-grade: enterprise GenAI gets a reliability-style eval frame

Ali et al.’s EnterpriseVal is the closest thing I’ve seen to an attempt at bringing engineering qualification thinking to enterprise generative AI. The move I like: the “evaluation object” isn’t a model—it’s a frozen socio-technical configuration (model + prompts + retrieval/tools + guardrails + human review) tied to a specific use case and local ground truth. That’s exactly how these systems fail in practice.

They also introduce an autonomy × consequence matrix to scale evaluation intensity. That’s basically a risk-based control plan for AI.

Where it gets very QE-friendly is the metric set: not just “accuracy,” but things like pass^k across repeated runs (stability), reviewer catch rate and false acceptance (oversight effectiveness), and explicit time/cost per successful task (value). The grading protocol—blinded experts plus LLM-as-judge corrected with prediction-powered inference—aims at making human evaluation cheaper without pretending it’s free.

Skeptical note: their pilot numbers (e.g., citation precision 88%, hallucination rate 1.6% in a credit memo workflow; big estimated hours saved in procedure transformation) are intriguing, but they themselves admit the uncomfortable part: no sample sizes, CIs, inter-rater agreement, or repeated-run rigor were recorded. So treat it as a strong framework with an illustrative pilot—not yet a qualification report.

Sparse longitudinal forecasting: accuracy is easy; reliable intervals are the real product

Kong et al. build a carefully QC’d benchmark for lesion-size forecasting with sparse CT follow-ups—five visits per trajectory, patient-level splits, and a fixed horizon design (predicting the same visit-to-visit change). That design choice matters: it prevents “easy horizons” from masquerading as model skill.

Two practitioner takeaways:

1. Most of the value is in the most recent extra observation. RMSE improves from m=1 to m=2, then flattens (and even worsens slightly). If you’re designing a monitoring schedule, that’s the kind of result you can act on.

2. Interval reliability isn’t the same as probabilistic calibration. Methods had near-perfect raw 95% coverage (some essentially 1.00), but PIT errors and NLL still varied. Conformal calibration helps coverage, but it doesn’t magically make the distribution “right.” If you’re using forecasts to trigger interventions, you want both coverage and sensible sharpness/likelihood behavior.

Also worth noting: their Gompertz-inspired regularizer mostly didn’t help; CV picked λ=0. A nice reminder that “biologically inspired” constraints can become accuracy taxes.

Rare-event reliability: importance sampling meets flows, with a “don’t collapse” mechanism

Helal et al. push adaptive importance sampling using mixtures of normalizing flows (FAMIS) for tiny failure probabilities. The clever bit is engineering around what usually breaks these methods: multimodal failure regions and mode collapse.

They combine (i) a defensive heavy-tailed exploration component (good early coverage), (ii) an annealed surrogate for the failure indicator (so you can learn without seeing failures), and (iii) a repulsion term (JSD) to keep mixture components from piling onto one mode. Reported results show stability and accuracy even into high dimensions where some baselines degrade, with a predictable evaluation budget N_{call}=KT+K_{est}. If you’re spending money on limit-state calls, that budget predictability is a feature, not a footnote.

A “reliability” paper that’s really about label noise (still useful)

Akhtar et al.’s Barge isn’t reliability-of-systems, but it is about reliability of supervision: imbalanced classification under noisy labels. The bounded, redescending loss is the practical idea—when a label looks confidently wrong, it stops dominating training. If you’ve got inspection labels, field-return codes, or human dispositions with known contamination, that’s directly relevant.

What to ponder this week

Across domains, the trend is the same: we’re moving from point performance to decision reliability—repeatability, calibrated uncertainty, oversight effectiveness, and cost-to-evidence. The open question for us: What’s the gen‑AI equivalent of an MSA report with confidence bounds and ongoing stability monitoring—and who in the org owns it?

  • Kong et al.: Reliability-Centered Evaluation of Sparse Longitudinal CT Lesion-Size Forecasting with Conformal Interval Calibration and Gompertz-Inspired Regularization (Reliability)
  • Helal et al.: Repulsive normalizing flow mixtures for adaptive importance sampling: reliability analysis of complex systems (Reliability)
